_note: Sensitosis Normie test bank: everyday detectors, no medicine. Same format as tests.json, plus yes/no (plural nouns for cases with and without the thing), all (plural noun for everything), pos/neg (verbs for flagged/cleared). kind: gadget | software | animal | human | check. sens = catches it when it's there; spec = stays quiet when it isn't. v = figure used for the reveal; lo/hi = range that scores full marks. spec null = sensitivity-only round. Every figure was read from the linked page; each entry's checked field gives the date.

aidet.scenario: A teacher feeds a stack of essays into the free AI-text classifier OpenAI released in January 2023.
aidet.says: It caught about 1 in 4 AI texts and wrongly accused about 1 in 11 human ones. OpenAI switched it off six months later for its ‘low rate of accuracy’. Points for honesty.
aidet.note: OpenAI’s own challenge set of English texts. Retired on 20 July 2023.
src: OpenAI: New AI classifier for indicating AI-written text (2023)

turnitin.test: Turnitin AI-writing detector (the company’s own figures)
turnitin.scenario: A uni assignment goes through Turnitin, which now gives an ‘AI-written’ percentage alongside the plagiarism check.
turnitin.says: On paper, miles better than OpenAI’s effort: it says it may miss up to 15% of AI text and wrongly flags under 1% of fully human work. Those are the company’s own numbers, not an independent test, and it says not to use the score alone.
turnitin.note: Turnitin’s published claims, as reported by Purdue University (2024). It only flags text when it is ‘98% sure’.
src: Purdue University: Turnitin adding AI writing detection, but use it with caution (2024)

fingerprint.test: Fingerprint expert matching a crime-scene print
fingerprint.scenario: A smudgy print lifted from a crime scene is compared with a known print by a trained examiner.
fingerprint.says: Wrong matches were very rare, about 1 in 1,000. Missed matches were far more common, about 1 in 13, and 85% of examiners missed at least one. Having a second examiner recheck caught all the wrong matches.
fingerprint.note: The FBI-backed ‘black box’ study (Ulery 2011, PNAS): 169 examiners, about 100 print pairs each.
src: Phys.org: False positives rare from fingerprint examiners (2011)

bedfield.test: Bed bug sniffer dog, in real apartments
bedfield.scenario: A trained beagle and handler sweep through apartments with real, natural infestations.
bedfield.says: In the real world the dogs found under half the bugs, and false alarms averaged 15%. Teams ranged from finding 10% to 100%, so it’s about the handler as much as the nose.
bedfield.note: Cooper, Wang and Singh 2014, Journal of Economic Entomology: 11 dog teams in naturally infested apartments.
src: Cooper et al. 2014: Accuracy of trained canines for detecting bed bugs (Rutgers PDF)

bedlab.test: Bed bug sniffer dog, in a set-up test room
bedlab.scenario: Researchers hide bed bugs in hotel rooms, then send in a trained dog to find them.
bedlab.says: Exam conditions, top marks: 98% found, zero false alarms. Then the same kind of dogs went into real apartments. See the other version. Practice is not the match.
bedlab.note: Pfiester 2008 controlled hotel-room hides, as reported in Cooper et al. 2014.
src: Cooper et al. 2014: Accuracy of trained canines for detecting bed bugs (Rutgers PDF)

polygraph.scenario: A suspect is wired up. Breathing, sweat and blood pressure are tracked while an examiner asks questions.
polygraph.says: Better than a coin toss, worse than its TV reputation. Roughly 1 in 5 honest people fail. In the US National Academies’ spy-screening example, a test that was 99.5% ‘correct’ overall still let 8 of 10 spies through.
polygraph.note: US National Research Council review (2003). A US Defense polygraph study gave about 85% and 78%; across lab studies, the catch rate ranged widely depending on how many false alarms you accept (10–30%).
src: National Academies: The Polygraph and Lie Detection (2003), chapter 5

humanlie.scenario: Someone tells you a story. You watch their face, listen to their voice and decide: lie or truth?
humanlie.says: Across more than 24,000 people in over 200 studies, we caught under half the lies, and got 54% right overall. Slightly better than a coin. We lean towards believing people, which is nice, if not great detective work.
humanlie.note: Bond and DePaulo 2006 meta-analysis, Personality and Social Psychology Review: 24,483 judges.
src: Bond and DePaulo 2006: Accuracy of deception judgments (PDF)

lineupsim.test: Police line-up, all faces at once
lineupsim.scenario: A witness looks at six faces side by side. Sometimes the culprit is there, sometimes not.
lineupsim.says: With the culprit there, witnesses picked them about half the time. With the culprit absent, most still picked someone. Memory badly wants to help, even when it can’t.
lineupsim.note: Steblay, Dysart and Wells 2011 meta-analysis of 72 lab tests. ‘Stays quiet’ means the witness says the culprit isn’t there.
src: Steblay, Dysart and Wells 2011: line-up meta-analysis (PDF)

lineupseq.test: Police line-up, one face at a time
lineupseq.scenario: Same witness, new method: faces are shown one by one, with a yes or no for each.
lineupseq.says: One at a time catches fewer culprits but makes far fewer wrong picks when the culprit isn’t there. A trade-off, not a free lunch.
lineupseq.note: Steblay, Dysart and Wells 2011 meta-analysis: 72 tests overall, 27 in the strictest subset.
src: Steblay, Dysart and Wells 2011: line-up meta-analysis (PDF)

tsa.condition: a smuggled weapon or fake bomb
tsa.scenario: 2015: undercover government ‘red teams’ pose as passengers and try to sneak banned items through US airport checkpoints.
tsa.says: The checkpoints stopped 3 of 70. That’s a 95% fail rate. Your water bottle never stood a chance, though.
tsa.note: US Homeland Security covert tests, confirmed by a government official in June 2015.
src: Fox13 / CNN: TSA screeners failed 67 of 70 undercover tests (2015)

captcha.scenario: A website makes you type squiggly letters to prove you’re not a robot.
captcha.says: Bots solved these almost every time, in under a second. Humans got 50 to 84% right and took up to 15 seconds. So the robot test mostly blocks… people.
captcha.note: Searles et al. 2023, ‘An Empirical Study and Evaluation of Modern CAPTCHAs’: 1,400 people. Bot accuracy was ‘just under 100%’, so anything from 0 to 5 scores full marks.
src: TechXplore: Bots are better at CAPTCHA than humans (2023)

pas.scenario: Night-time traffic stop. The officer chats through the window holding a torch with a built-in alcohol sensor. No blowing required.
pas.says: Catches about 3 in 4 drivers over the US 0.08 limit just from their breath in the air, and almost never flags a sober driver. Plot twist: in this study, handing out the torches didn’t change the arrest rate at all.
pas.note: Field figures (6 of 9 bars) cited in Fell, Compton and Voas 2008, Traffic Injury Prevention. Australia’s usual limit is lower, 0.05.
src: Fell, Compton and Voas 2008: passive alcohol sensors at traffic stops (PMC)

facerec.scenario: London: a camera on a police van scans faces in a busy street and checks them against a watchlist.
facerec.says: Catches about 9 in 10 people on the list and wrongly flags about 1 in 6,000 passers-by. Tiny, until 60,000 people walk past. At looser settings than the default, false alarms weren’t shared equally: Black faces were wrongly flagged more often.
facerec.note: UK National Physical Laboratory testing for the Met and South Wales Police (2023), at the default 0.6 setting.
src: The Register: UK police facial recognition test results (2023)

smoke.test: Home smoke alarm in a real fire
smoke.scenario: A fire breaks out at home, big enough to set off an alarm. There’s an alarm on the ceiling. Does it go off?
smoke.says: It went off in 88% of fires. But in fires where someone died and an alarm was present, it sounded only 71% of the time. And for the record: 73% of people said the last time theirs went off, it was cooking.
smoke.note: US National Fire Protection Association report (Jan 2019), 2012–2016 home fires. No good figure for false alarms, so one slider today.
src: NFPA: Smoke Alarms in US Home Fires (2019, PDF)

bombdog.scenario: 56 dog-and-handler teams search test areas with hidden explosives. These figures are for the top eight.
bombdog.says: Even the best teams found about 8 in 10, short of the official 90% standard. None of the 56 teams met it. Very good dogs, very tough exam.
bombdog.note: DeGreeff, Prada-Tiedemann et al. 2025, Frontiers in Veterinary Science. The standard asks for 90% found and under 10% false alerts.
src: Frontiers news: explosive detection dogs assessment (2025)

koaladog.scenario: Queensland: a trained detection dog searches the bush for koala droppings, so researchers can tell where koalas live without seeing one.
koaladog.says: Found the droppings in 146 of 150 trials, and every time once off the lead. In the field, the dog team was 19 times faster than people searching on foot. Good dog. Very good dog.
koaladog.note: Cristescu et al. 2015, Scientific Reports: one detection dog, Maya, tested on hidden koala scats. No false-alert figure was reported, so one slider today.
src: Cristescu et al. 2015: Accuracy and efficiency of detection dogs for koala conservation (Scientific Reports)

sharkplane.test: Beach shark patrol, from a plane
sharkplane.scenario: NSW: a light plane flies the coast looking down for sharks near the beach. Researchers put shark-shaped dummies in a clear bay to see how many the spotters find.
sharkplane.says: The plane crew spotted about 1 in 8 dummy sharks. A helicopter did a little better, about 1 in 6. The ocean is big, glare is real and sharks don’t wave.
sharkplane.note: Robbins, Peddemors, Kennelly et al. (PLOS ONE, 2014), first prepared for the NSW Government: fixed-wing 12.5%, helicopter 17.1%. One slider today.
src: InDaily: Aerial patrols miss most sharks, new research (2013)

tornado.scenario: Somewhere in Oklahoma, the US National Weather Service watches the radar. Does a tornado that actually touches down get a warning first?
tornado.says: About 7 in 10 tornadoes got a warning, up from 3 in 10 in the 1980s. The catch: nearly 3 in 4 warnings were false alarms, which is how people learn to ignore the siren.
tornado.note: NWS verification data for the decade to 2014, as reported by FiveThirtyEight. One slider today; the false-alarm figure is a share of warnings, not of quiet days.
src: FiveThirtyEight: Three out of every four tornado warnings are false alarms

gmail.scenario: Your inbox. Machine learning decides which emails are junk or scams before you ever see them.
gmail.says: Google says it blocks 99.9% of spam and phishing. Sounds perfect, until you remember billions arrive a day, so 0.1% is still a lot of ‘you’ve won a prize’. Google doesn’t publish how much real mail it wrongly bins.
gmail.note: Google’s own figure (2018), not an independent test. One slider today.
src: BleepingComputer: Google says Gmail now blocks 99.9 percent of spam and phishing emails

weather.scenario: The Bureau of Meteorology tells you tomorrow’s top will be 27 °C. How often does the real top land within 2 degrees?
weather.says: Within 2 °C about 9 days in 10. Overnight lows are trickier, 84%. And today’s 2-day forecast is about as good as a 1-day forecast was ten years ago.
weather.note: Bureau of Meteorology forecast verification, next-day maximum temperature. One slider today.
src: Bureau of Meteorology: Understanding forecast accuracy and verification

passport.test: Passport officer checking a photo ID
passport.scenario: Australia: working passport officers compare a real person standing in front of them with the photo on their ID card. Sometimes the photo is of someone else who looks similar.
passport.says: They let through 14% of fakes and wrongly rejected 6% of real IDs. Years on the job made no difference. Faces of strangers are much harder than we think.
passport.note: White, Kemp, Jenkins, Matheson and Burton (PLOS ONE, 2014): 30 Australian passport officers, person-to-photo test.
src: White et al.: Passport officers' errors in face matching (PLOS ONE, 2014, PDF)

pigeonsea.scenario: 1970s–80s, Project Sea Hunt: pigeons trained to peck a key when they see an orange life jacket ride in a bubble under a US Coast Guard helicopter.
pigeonsea.says: The pigeons spotted the target on the first pass about 9 times in 10, and usually before the humans on board did.
pigeonsea.note: US Coast Guard Project Sea Hunt results, as reported by We Are The Mighty. One slider today.
src: We Are The Mighty: That time the Coast Guard tried using pigeons for sea rescues

crewsea.scenario: 1970s–80s: in US Coast Guard search trials, trained helicopter crew look out for an orange life jacket bobbing on the water.
crewsea.says: The crew found it on the first pass only 38% of the time. Told they were racing trained pigeons (which managed about 90%), they lifted to about 50%.
crewsea.note: US Coast Guard Project Sea Hunt, as reported by We Are The Mighty. Anything from 38 to 50 scores full marks.
src: We Are The Mighty: That time the Coast Guard tried using pigeons for sea rescues

faceid.scenario: Someone picks up your iPhone and holds it up to their face. Do they get in?
faceid.says: Apple puts the odds of a random stranger getting in at under 1 in a million. The fine print: the odds are higher for twins, lookalike siblings and kids under 13. Ask any parent of twins.
faceid.note: Apple’s own figure, for a single enrolled appearance. One slider today: anything from 99.9 scores full marks.
src: Apple Support: About Face ID advanced technology

termitedog.scenario: Florida: trained dogs sniff a row of sealed containers. Some hide live termites, some hide wood, termite-damaged timber or nothing at all.
termitedog.says: The dogs found termites in about 96% of the containers that had them, and wrongly sat at under 3% of the empty ones. They could even tell live termites from damaged wood.
termitedog.note: University of Florida study (Brooks, Oi and Koehler, Journal of Economic Entomology, 2003), as reported by PCT magazine: 95.93% found, 2.69% false indications.
src: PCT: Focus on termite control, top dog

wine.test: Your taste buds, spotting the pricey wine
wine.scenario: Edinburgh Science Festival, 2011: members of the public taste a wine under £5 and one from £10 to £30. Which is the posh one?
wine.says: Exactly 50%: a coin toss. Whites came in at 53%, reds 47%. The wine trade was not amused. Pour yourself the cheap one.
wine.note: Prof Richard Wiseman’s blind tasting, over 500 people. One slider today: anything from 47 to 53 scores full marks.
src: Edinburgh Guide: Expensive wines don’t win out in mass taste test (2011)

fakereviewhuman.test: Your gut, spotting a fake hotel review
fakereviewhuman.scenario: Researchers paid people to write glowing fake reviews of Chicago hotels, mixed them with real five-star ones, and asked readers to sort them.
fakereviewhuman.says: People caught only about 3 in 10 fakes. They were good at believing real reviews, mostly because they believed most of what they read. Trusting is lovely; it’s just not a detector.
fakereviewhuman.note: Ott, Choi, Cardie and Hancock (Cornell, 2011): three human judges, 160 reviews. Averages of the judges’ figures.
src: Ott et al.: Finding deceptive opinion spam by any stretch of the imagination (2011)

fakereviewbot.scenario: Researchers mixed paid-for fake five-star reviews of Chicago hotels with real ones, then let a computer program trained on writing style sort them.
fakereviewbot.says: About 9 in 10 both ways. Its tells: fakes talk more about ‘me’ and the trip, real ones about the room and the bathroom. Machines 1, humans 0.
fakereviewbot.note: Ott et al. (Cornell, 2011): best classifier 89.8% for both fake and real reviews.
src: Ott et al.: Finding deceptive opinion spam by any stretch of the imagination (2011)

aiface.test: Your eyes, real face or AI face?
aiface.scenario: People are shown faces one at a time. Some are real photos, some were made by AI. Real or fake?
aiface.says: 48%, worse than a coin toss. A bit of training lifted it to 59%. And people rated the AI faces as slightly more trustworthy than the real ones.
aiface.note: Nightingale and Farid (PNAS, 2022). One slider today: anything from 48 to 59 scores full marks.
src: AI News: Humans struggle to distinguish real and AI-generated faces (2022)

offside.scenario: English Premier League: the assistant referee sprints along the line and decides, in a split second, whether to raise the flag.
offside.says: About 82 in 100. At the 2002 World Cup it was closer to 74. Your eyes simply can’t track two players and the moment of the pass at once. Go easy on the person with the flag.
offside.note: Journal of Sports Sciences (2010), as reported by Soccer Referee USA. One slider today.
src: Soccer Referee USA: Study, ARs make too many inaccurate offside decisions (2019)

firearms.test: Firearms expert matching a cartridge case
firearms.condition: a case fired from the same gun
firearms.scenario: US crime-lab examiners compare marks on spent cartridge cases under a microscope. Same gun or different gun?
firearms.says: Very good overall: about 1 in 100 different-gun pairs was wrongly called a match. But 20 of the 22 wrong matches came from just 5 of the 218 examiners. The average hides the outliers.
firearms.note: Baldwin et al., Ames Laboratory black-box study (2014): false positives 22 of 2,178; 4 eliminations and 11 inconclusives among 1,090 same-gun pairs.
src: Baldwin et al.: A study of false-positive and false-negative error rates in cartridge case comparisons (2014, PDF)

quakealert.scenario: Millions of Android phones act as tiny seismometers. When enough of them shake at once, Google sends a warning.
quakealert.says: 85% of people who felt a quake got an alert, and over a third got it before the shaking reached them. Over 1,200 alerts, only three were false: two thunderstorms and one mass notification.
quakealert.note: Google’s study in Science (July 2025), 2021–2024, as reported by Live Science. One slider today.
src: Live Science: Google has turned 2 billion smartphones into an earthquake warning system (2025)

lightning.condition: a lightning strike to the ground
lightning.scenario: A network of sensors across the US listens for the radio crackle of lightning and pins down where each bolt hit.
lightning.says: Better than 95% of cloud-to-ground flashes get picked up. It can also tell a ground strike from cloud-to-cloud lightning about 9 times in 10.
lightning.note: Vaisala, operator of the US National Lightning Detection Network (2021). One slider today: 95 or above scores full marks.
src: Vaisala: AI upgrade to the National Lightning Detection Network (2021)

voicefake.test: Your ears, spotting a fake voice
voicefake.scenario: People listen to short voice clips in English or Mandarin. Some are real, some were made by AI. Can they hear the fake?
voicefake.says: About 73%: more than a quarter of fakes got through. Training barely helped. And voice cloning has only got better since. A family code word is cheap insurance.
voicefake.note: Mai et al., University College London (PLOS ONE, 2023): 529 people. One slider today.
src: UCL: Humans unable to detect over a quarter of deepfake speech samples (2023)

umpire.test: Baseball umpire, calling balls and strikes
umpire.scenario: Major League Baseball: the plate umpire decides if each pitch the batter didn’t swing at was a strike or a ball.
umpire.says: Roughly 4 in 5. With two strikes on the batter it dropped to about 71%. That added up to over 34,000 wrong calls in 2018: about 14 a game. Robot umpires, anyone?
umpire.note: Boston University analysis of nearly 4 million pitches over 11 seasons (2019), via The Conversation. One slider today.
src: The Conversation: An analysis of nearly 4 million pitches shows how many mistakes umpires make (2019)

gorilla.condition: a person in a gorilla suit
gorilla.scenario: You’re counting basketball passes in a video. Halfway through, someone in a gorilla suit strolls through the middle of the game.
gorilla.says: Under half noticed. When the gorilla stopped and thumped its chest, it was still only 50%. Focus is a spotlight, and everything outside it goes dark.
gorilla.note: Simons and Chabris, ‘Gorillas in our midst’ (Perception, 1999): 192 people. One slider today: 42 to 50 scores full marks.

doorswap.test: Your eyes, noticing a swapped stranger
doorswap.scenario: A stranger stops you to ask for directions. Two workers carry a door between you, and behind it the stranger is replaced by someone else. You carry on giving directions.
doorswap.says: Only 7 of 15 people noticed they were talking to someone new, despite a different height, voice and clothes. Change blindness: we keep a much rougher picture of the world than it feels.
doorswap.note: Simons and Levin (Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 1998), experiment 1. One slider today.
src: Simons and Levin: Failure to detect changes to people during a real-world interaction (1998, PDF)

ownname.test: Your ears, catching your own name
ownname.condition: your name, said in the other ear
ownname.scenario: Headphones on. You repeat words played to one ear and ignore the other. Partway through, the ignored ear says your name.
ownname.says: About a third. The famous ‘cocktail party effect’ is real, but it’s not everyone. Oddly, people with less working memory were more likely to catch their name.
ownname.note: Conway, Cowan and Bunting (Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 2001), repeating Moray’s 1959 finding. One slider today.
src: Conway et al.: The cocktail party phenomenon revisited (2001)

rareitem.test: Bag-screening search, when the item is rare
rareitem.scenario: Volunteers search X-ray-style images of packed bags for a tool. Only 1 bag in 100 actually has one.
rareitem.says: They missed about 30% of rare tools. When half the bags had one, misses fell to about 7%. If you rarely find anything, your brain starts to quit early.
rareitem.note: Wolfe, Horowitz and Kenner (Nature, 2005), as reported by NPR. One slider today.
src: NPR: Rare items often missed in visual searches (2005)

snakedog.scenario: Guam: invasive brown tree snakes hide in trees and rock piles. Detector dogs search patches of forest where a radio-tagged snake is hiding.
snakedog.says: About 35%. The more experienced team found 44%, the newer one 26%. The researchers still rated dogs as useful next to people searching by eye in daylight.
snakedog.note: Savidge et al., US Geological Survey (2011): 85 trials over four months. One slider today: 26 to 44 scores full marks.
src: USGS: Canine detection of free-ranging brown treesnakes on Guam (2011)

teachers.scenario: Experienced school teachers read a mix of student essays and ones written by ChatGPT. Which are which?
teachers.says: They caught only about 38% of the AI essays, and called more than a quarter of genuine student essays AI.
teachers.note: Fleckenstein et al. (Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, 2024): 200 experienced teachers.
src: Fleckenstein et al.: Do teachers spot AI? (2024)

groundhog.scenario: 2 February, Pennsylvania: a groundhog either sees his shadow (six more weeks of winter) or doesn’t (an early spring). Crowds turn up to watch.
groundhog.says: About 35 in 100, worse than tossing a coin. When NOAA ranked 19 groundhog-style forecasters over 20 years, Phil came 17th. Still the most famous, though.
groundhog.note: NOAA’s grading against US March temperatures, 2005–2024, as reported in 2025. One slider today.
src: WJLA: Punxsutawney Phil’s not-so-legendary forecasts, NOAA study reveals
groundhog.label: Animal forecaster

octopus.test: Paul the Octopus, picking football winners
octopus.scenario: A German aquarium, 2008–2010: before each match, Paul gets two boxes of food, each marked with a team’s flag. Whichever box he opens first is his pick.
octopus.says: 12 out of 14, including all 8 at the 2010 World Cup, final and all. A lovely lesson in small samples: with enough animals guessing, one is bound to look psychic.
octopus.note: Paul’s full record across Euro 2008 and the 2010 World Cup. One slider today.
octopus.label: Animal forecaster

autobrake.scenario: AAA testing, 2019: a child-sized dummy darts out from between two parked cars in front of a car doing 20 mph (32 km/h). Does automatic emergency braking stop in time?
autobrake.says: Only 1 run in 10. With two adult dummies the cars hit them 80% of the time, they hit every dummy when turning, and AAA said the systems didn’t work at night. Brakes still work best with a human foot on them.
autobrake.note: AAA (American Automobile Association) tests of 2019 cars with pedestrian detection, reported by CBS News. One slider today.
src: CBS News: AAA says automatic braking systems meant to save pedestrians fail in nearly every test (2019)

vsa.scenario: A US county jail: recently arrested men are asked about recent drug use while voice-analysis software listens for stress. A drug test later shows who lied.
vsa.says: It caught about 15 lies in 100 (one program 21, the other 8) and cleared about 91 in 100 honest answers. Overall about 50% accurate: a coin toss with a microphone.
vsa.note: US National Institute of Justice field test (2008): 319 arrestees in the Oklahoma County jail, two programs (CVSA and LVA).
src: NIJ: Voice stress analysis, only 15 percent of lies about drug use detected in field test

subwayscan.test: AI weapons scanner, versus innocent riders
subwayscan.scenario: New York, 2024: AI-powered walk-through weapons scanners are trialled at 20 subway stations for 30 days. Nearly everyone is unarmed. How many walk straight through?
subwayscan.says: About 96 in 100. Sounds fine until you do the maths: 2,749 scans, 118 false alarms and zero guns found (12 knives, though). So every alarm for a gun was a false one.
subwayscan.note: NYPD figures from the 2024 pilot (4.29% false positives), reported by AP via ABC News. One slider today.
src: ABC News (AP): AI-powered weapons scanners used in NYC subway found zero guns in one-month test (2024)

toefl.test: AI-writing detectors, on non-native English essays
toefl.scenario: Seven popular AI-text detectors check 91 essays written by real students for the TOEFL English exam.
toefl.says: Only about 39 in 100. The detectors flagged 61% as AI-written. All seven wrongly agreed on nearly 1 in 5, and 97% were flagged by at least one. Essays by US eighth-graders sailed through: plainer wording looks ‘machine-like’ to these tools.
toefl.note: Stanford study (Liang et al., 2023), reported by Stanford HAI. One slider today.
src: Stanford HAI: AI-detectors biased against non-native English writers (2023)

burglar.scenario: A monitored burglar alarm goes off and police are called out.
burglar.pos: turn out to be a real break-in
burglar.neg: turn out to be false alarms
burglar.says: Somewhere between 2 and 6 in 100. Between 94% and 98% of alarm calls are false: think pets, wind, wobbly doors and owners who forgot the code.
burglar.note: US Center for Problem-Oriented Policing guide to false burglar alarms. One slider today.
src: Center for Problem-Oriented Policing: False burglar alarms

recaptcha.test: Image-grid CAPTCHA, versus an AI bot
recaptcha.scenario: ‘Select all squares with traffic lights.’ Researchers at ETH Zurich point a trained image AI at Google’s reCAPTCHA v2 picture puzzles.
recaptcha.says: Zero. The AI solved 100% of the image puzzles, up from 68–71% for earlier bots. These days the grid mostly tests whether you’re patient.
recaptcha.note: Plesner, Vontobel and Wattenhofer (2024), reported by TechRadar. One slider today.
src: TechRadar: This AI tool can solve Google’s popular anti-spam defence every time (2024)

beagle.scenario: A US airport arrivals hall: a beagle works the baggage carousel, sniffing for undeclared food that could carry pests and plant diseases.
beagle.says: About 90 in 100 for a beagle with two years’ experience. Rookies, at 6–12 months on the job, manage about 80. Experience counts, even for beagles.
beagle.note: US Department of Agriculture fact sheet on its ‘Beagle Brigade’ detector dogs. One slider today.
src: USDA APHIS: Detector dogs (archived fact sheet)

mushroomapp.test: Mushroom ID app, on poisonous mushrooms
mushroomapp.scenario: Researchers photograph 78 wild mushrooms, deadly ones included, and run the photos through three popular identification apps.
mushroomapp.says: The best app (Picture Mushroom) named only 44% of the poisonous ones correctly; the others managed 30–40%. Overall the best app was right 49% of the time. Never eat anything on an app’s say-so.
mushroomapp.note: Comparison of Picture Mushroom, Mushroom Identificator and iNaturalist (2023), PubMed abstract. One slider today.
src: PubMed: A comparison of the accuracy of mushroom identification applications using digital photographs (2023)

inatmushroom.scenario: The same 78 wild mushroom photos go through iNaturalist, the popular nature-ID app.
inatmushroom.says: About 35 in 100 overall (40% for the poisonous ones). Great for birds and bugs; fungi are famously tricky even for experts.
inatmushroom.note: Comparison of three mushroom apps (2023), PubMed abstract. One slider today.
src: PubMed: A comparison of the accuracy of mushroom identification applications using digital photographs (2023)

newt.test: Pond-water DNA test for great crested newts
newt.scenario: UK: instead of night-time torch surveys, a scoop of pond water is tested for traces of DNA the newts shed into the water (eDNA).
newt.says: About 99 in 100 in the detailed study of 35 ponds, better than any combination of traditional methods. Volunteers collecting their own samples got 91%.
newt.note: Freshwater Habitats Trust, on the 35-pond study in Hampshire and North Wales and the 2013 volunteer pilot. One slider today.
src: Freshwater Habitats Trust: PondNet eDNA surveys
newt.label: Water DNA test

tennischallenge.scenario: A ball lands near the line and the player is certain the call is wrong. They challenge, and Hawk-Eye’s replay decides.
tennischallenge.says: Only about 46 in 100. Players are sure they saw it; Hawk-Eye disagrees more often than not. Eyes, adrenaline and wishful thinking.
tennischallenge.note: An analysis of player challenges, cited by Topend Sports. One slider today.

var.scenario: English Premier League: big refereeing calls now get a second look from the video assistant referee (VAR).
var.says: About 96 in 100, up from 82 before VAR. That last 4% still fuels a lot of Saturday shouting.
var.note: Premier League figures reported by Sky Sports (February 2024). One slider today.
src: Sky Sports: Premier League claims 96 per cent of referee decisions are correct (2024)
var.label: Human + video

prevar.scenario: English Premier League, before video replays: the referee and assistants make every big call live, at full speed.
prevar.says: About 82 in 100. Not bad at full speed with 22 players in the way, but nearly 1 in 5 big calls wrong is why VAR arrived (and took it to 96).
prevar.note: Premier League figures reported by Sky Sports (February 2024). One slider today.
src: Sky Sports: Premier League claims 96 per cent of referee decisions are correct (2024)

touchid.test: Touch ID, versus a stranger’s finger
touchid.scenario: Someone else presses their finger on your iPhone’s home button. Do they get in?
touchid.says: Apple puts the odds of someone else’s fingerprint unlocking your phone at 1 in 50,000. Face ID is 1 in a million, so your face is 20 times pickier than your thumb.
touchid.note: Apple’s figures, reported by How-To Geek. One slider today: anything from 99.9 scores full marks.
src: How-To Geek: How secure are Face ID and Touch ID?

deepfakeai.condition: the right answer, real or fake
deepfakeai.scenario: 2020: Facebook’s Deepfake Detection Challenge. Over 2,000 entrants build AI to spot face-swapped videos. The winner is tested on a secret set of fresh clips.
deepfakeai.says: About 65 in 100 on the unseen videos. On the practice set, the top model scored 82.56%. Real life is always harder than the practice set.
deepfakeai.note: Meta AI: Deepfake Detection Challenge results (2020): 2,114 participants, over 35,000 models. One slider today.
src: Meta AI: Deepfake Detection Challenge results (2020)

snapper.scenario: 2018: the ocean charity Oceana buys fish from restaurants and shops across the US and DNA-tests it.
snapper.neg: turn out to be another fish
snapper.says: Only 58 in 100: 42% of ‘snapper’ was something else, and sea bass was wrong 55% of the time. Overall 1 in 5 fish was mislabelled, more in restaurants (26%) than big supermarkets (12%).
snapper.note: Oceana DNA tests of 449 fish in 24 US states and Washington DC, March–August 2018. One slider today.
src: Oceana: Seafood fraud persists, more than 20% of samples mislabeled (2019)
snapper.label: Label check

oliveoil.scenario: 2010: researchers buy imported olive oil labelled ‘extra virgin’ in California and send it for the official taste and chemical tests (done in Australia, as it happens).
oliveoil.says: Only 31 in 100. 69% of the imported samples failed extra virgin standards, against 10% of the Californian ones. Fourteen imported brands were tested.
oliveoil.note: UC Davis Olive Center study (2010), using International Olive Council methods. One slider today.
src: UC Davis: Most imported olive oils don’t match ‘extra virgin’ claims, study finds (2010)
oliveoil.label: Label check

merlin.test: Merlin bird app, naming birds by song
merlin.scenario: Birdwatchers and the free Merlin Sound ID app listen at the same survey spots. When the app names a species, is it actually there?
merlin.says: 86 in 100, close to human birders’ 92. But it heard far less: people logged 382 detections to Merlin’s 222. Good at what it hears, deaf to a lot.
merlin.note: Field point-count study reported by the American Ornithological Society. Merlin made 12 false species IDs. One slider today.
src: American Ornithological Society: Humans outperform Merlin Sound ID in field-based point-count surveys

birder.test: Human birder, naming birds by ear
birder.scenario: The same survey spots, but this time a trained human birder listens. When they name a species, is it really there?
birder.says: 92 in 100, a touch better than the Merlin app’s 86. And people noticed far more birds: 382 detections to Merlin’s 222.
birder.note: Field point-count study reported by the American Ornithological Society. One slider today.
src: American Ornithological Society: Humans outperform Merlin Sound ID in field-based point-count surveys

sobriety.scenario: A US traffic stop: the officer has the driver follow a pen with their eyes, walk heel-to-toe and stand on one leg. Over 0.08, the US limit, or not?
sobriety.says: The official figure: officers were right 91% of the time using all three tests (eyes alone 88%, one leg 83%, walk-and-turn 79%). Independent statisticians later argued accuracy is much worse near the limit.
sobriety.note: US road safety agency (NHTSA) validation study, Stuster and Burns (1998), as cited in Illinois training material; plus a later statistical critique. One slider today.
src: University of Illinois Springfield: SFST training material (PDF)
PubMed: Statistical evaluation of standardized field sobriety tests

shakealert.scenario: California, Oregon and Washington: ShakeAlert issues an alert for a magnitude 4.5+ quake, seconds before the shaking arrives.
shakealert.says: 94 of 95 alerts were for real earthquakes (Oct 2019–Sep 2023). A few put the quake in the wrong place, but it almost never invented one.
shakealert.note: USGS: Status and performance of the ShakeAlert system, 2019–2023. One slider today.
src: USGS: Status and performance of ShakeAlert earthquake early warning system, 2019–2023

speech.scenario: You dictate a message to your phone and Google’s speech recognition turns it into text.
speech.says: About 95 in 100: a word error rate of 4.9%, down from 23% in 2013. Still roughly one wrong word every couple of sentences.
speech.note: Google I/O 2017, reported by VentureBeat. One slider today.
src: VentureBeat: Google’s speech recognition technology now has a 4.9% word error rate (2017)

nswdogs.test: Police drug dog, sitting next to someone
nswdogs.scenario: NSW, 2017: a police drug dog sits beside someone, and police search them.
nswdogs.says: Only 36 in 100. Of 1,124 people strip-searched after a dog indication in 2017, drugs were found 406 times. That’s 718 searches that turned up nothing.
nswdogs.note: NSW Police figures for 2017, reported by The New Daily. One slider today.
src: The New Daily: Sniffer dogs wrong in two-thirds of strip searches last year (2018)

tsunami.scenario: Before 1996: after a big undersea quake, the Pacific Tsunami Warning Center issues a warning and coasts evacuate.
tsunami.says: Only 1 in 4: 15 of 20 warnings had been false alarms. That’s why the US laid deep-ocean pressure sensors (DART buoys) that measure the wave itself.
tsunami.note: NOAA report on deep-ocean tsunami detectors (Milburn et al., 1996). One slider today.
src: NOAA: Real-time tsunami reporting from the deep ocean (Milburn et al., 1996)

phishing.test: Your eyes, spotting a phishing email
phishing.scenario: An online quiz shows real emails that look like they’re from PayPal, Amazon, Apple and others. Some are genuine, some are scams. Phish or legit?
phishing.says: People spotted about 85% of the scams but wrongly binned about 38% of the genuine emails. A real email from the shop Target was called a scam by 61%. Suspicion is healthy; checking the sender is better.
phishing.note: ESET quiz of over 20,000 Americans (2015). Figures average four scam and four genuine emails.
src: ESET: Can Americans catch a phish? 1 in 4 take the bait (2015)

bodyscanner.test: Airport body scanner, versus innocent passengers
bodyscanner.scenario: Hamburg airport, 2010–11: Germany trials full-body scanners on nearly 800,000 volunteer passengers.
bodyscanner.says: Only about 30 in 100. An internal report said the scanners sounded alerts 70% of the time, and the police union called them a failure.
bodyscanner.note: Hamburg airport trial, September 2010 to July 2011, as reported by The Local. One slider today.
src: The Local: ‘Naked’ body scanners a failure, police union says (2011)

lanternlab.test: Lanternfly-egg sniffer dog, in a test room
lanternlab.scenario: US: pet dogs and their owners train to sniff out egg masses of the spotted lanternfly, an invasive bug. First, a controlled scent test.
lanternlab.says: 82 in 100 in the controlled tests. Not bad for volunteers’ pet dogs: 182 teams were picked from over 1,000 keen owners.
lanternlab.note: University of Pennsylvania study (2025), reported by ScienceDaily. One slider today.
src: ScienceDaily: Dogs sniff out invasive spotted lanternfly eggs (2025)

lanternfield.test: Lanternfly-egg sniffer dog, out in the field
lanternfield.scenario: The same pet-dog teams now search real outdoor sites for the egg masses of the invasive spotted lanternfly.
lanternfield.says: 61 in 100 outdoors, down from 82 in the test room. Still better than many human searches, the researchers said.
lanternfield.note: University of Pennsylvania study (2025), reported by Virginia Tech and ScienceDaily. One slider today.
src: Virginia Tech CALS: Sniffing out the spotted lanternfly (2025)

fireant.scenario: Dogs are trained to find red imported fire ants, an invasive pest, even when other kinds of ants are around.
fireant.says: About 93 in 100 with other ant species mixed in, and over 98% when the sample held ten or more fire ants.
fireant.note: Lin et al. (2011), ‘Fire ant-detecting canines’, FAO AGRIS abstract. One slider today.
src: FAO AGRIS: Fire ant-detecting canines, a complementary method in detecting red imported fire ants

wildliferat.condition: pangolin scales, rhino horn and other wildlife
wildliferat.scenario: Dar es Salaam port, Tanzania, 2023: African giant pouched rats sniff shipping containers for hidden wildlife products.
wildliferat.says: 85 in 100, even sniffing through container vents. In the lab, eight trained rats still perfectly picked out pangolin, rhino horn and wood after eight months off.
wildliferat.note: APOPO study in Frontiers in Conservation Science, reported by Yale Environment 360 (2024). One slider today.
src: Yale Environment 360: Trained rats able to sniff out smuggled rhino horns (2024)

sharkspotter.scenario: NSW beaches: a drone streams video to SharkSpotter, AI software trained to pick out sharks.
sharkspotter.says: Over 90% accurate, said its makers at the University of Technology Sydney. Compare human spotters in helicopters (about 17%) and planes (12.5%).
sharkspotter.note: The SharkSpotter team writing in The Conversation (2018). One slider today.
src: The Conversation: SharkSpotter combines AI and drone technology to spot sharks (2018)

sharkheli.scenario: Human spotters in a helicopter fly along the beaches looking for sharks in the water below.
sharkheli.says: About 17 in 100. Spotters in planes managed 12.5%. Glare, waves and murky water hide a lot, which is why drones with AI are being tried.
sharkheli.note: Figures quoted by the SharkSpotter team in The Conversation (2018). One slider today.
src: The Conversation: SharkSpotter combines AI and drone technology to spot sharks (2018)

shotspotter.scenario: Chicago: microphones on poles pick up a bang, software decides it was gunfire, and police are sent.
shotspotter.pos: turn up evidence of a gun crime
shotspotter.says: About 9 in 100: roughly 4,500 gun-crime incidents from more than 50,000 alerts (2020–21), the city’s Inspector General found. The company says it is 97% accurate at detecting gunfire; turning a bang into evidence is another matter.
shotspotter.note: Chicago Office of Inspector General report, reported by Security Sales & Integration. One slider today.
src: Security Sales & Integration: Questions raised about accuracy of ShotSpotter gunshot detection

megadetector.scenario: Trail cameras snap thousands of pictures, most of them empty bush. Free AI software sorts the animal photos from the rest.
megadetector.says: 92 in 100 animal photos caught. But only 82% of the photos it flagged really had an animal in them. For people it caught 95% and was right 99% of the time. Saves researchers weeks of scrolling.
megadetector.note: Recreation-ecology study (bioRxiv preprint, 2022), at a 90% confidence setting. One slider today.
src: bioRxiv: Use of object detection in camera trap image identification (2022)

aiimage.test: Your eyes, real photo or AI image?
aiimage.condition: the right answer, real or AI
aiimage.scenario: Microsoft’s ‘Real or Not’ online quiz shows a mix of real photos and AI-generated images.
aiimage.says: 62 in 100, from about 287,000 guesses by 12,500 people worldwide. People did best on portraits and worst on landscapes and city scenes.
aiimage.note: Microsoft Research study of the ‘Real or Not’ quiz. One slider today.
src: Microsoft Research: How good are humans at detecting AI-generated images?

coalarm.scenario: UK, 2018: the consumer group Which? tests cheap carbon monoxide alarms sold on Amazon and eBay. All claim to meet the safety standard.
coalarm.says: The worst model failed to detect the gas in more than 80% of tests, so under 20 in 100. Three unbranded alarms also kept staying silent, and they were pulled from sale. Buy a known brand.
coalarm.note: Which? tests reported by ITV News (June 2018). One slider today.
src: ITV News: Dozens of carbon monoxide alarms taken off sale after failing tests (2018)

quolldog.scenario: Australia: dogs are trained to find the droppings of the endangered tiger quoll, a spotted marsupial hunter that’s rarely seen.
quolldog.says: Somewhere between 50 and 70 in 100 early in training, which the researchers called very high for such a rare animal.
quolldog.note: Report on Australian conservation detection dogs, phys.org (2017). One slider today.
src: phys.org: Australian dogs trained to sniff out endangered species (2017)

anpr.scenario: Queensland police cars carry cameras that read number plates automatically and check them against lists of stolen or unregistered cars.
anpr.says: Only about 19 in 100, the state’s auditor found in 2015. Plates are small, dirty and moving; the cameras were optimistic.
anpr.note: Queensland Audit Office report (2015), reported by iTnews. One slider today.
src: iTnews: Qld auditor slams accuracy of automated police cameras (2015)

nflchallenge.scenario: American football: a coach throws a red flag to challenge the referee’s call, and video replay decides.
nflchallenge.says: About 47 in 100 in the 2017 season (86 of 182). Coaches are convinced; the replay usually isn’t.
nflchallenge.note: Football Zebras, 2017 NFL regular season. One slider today.
src: Football Zebras: Reversals in replay dip after controversial season (2018)

winejudge.test: Wine show judge, tasting the same wine again
winejudge.scenario: California State Fair wine competition: without knowing it, judges are served the same wine more than once.
winejudge.says: Only about 10 in 100 judges regularly put the same wine in the same medal category. Separately, about 1 in 4 wines that won gold at one show won nothing at another.
winejudge.note: Robert Hodgson’s studies of the California State Fair, reported by The Globe and Mail. One slider today.
src: The Globe and Mail: Gold medal, passable plonk

cola.test: Your tongue, picking out the Coke
cola.scenario: A 1949 blind taste test: three unlabelled glasses of Coca-Cola, Pepsi and RC Cola. Which one is Coke?
cola.says: 41 in 100, barely above the 33% you’d get by guessing (Pepsi 38%, RC 35%). When all three glasses secretly held the same cola, people still confidently named them.
cola.note: Pronko and Bowles (1949), via JSTOR Daily. One slider today.
src: JSTOR Daily: The Coca-Cola wars, can anybody really tell the difference?

eyedetect.condition: the right answer, lie or truth
eyedetect.scenario: Instead of wires and a cuff, you answer true/false questions on a screen while a camera watches your eyes.
eyedetect.says: The company says 86% accurate. That’s its own figure, not an independent test, so file it next to the polygraph’s ‘it depends’.
eyedetect.note: EyeDetect maker’s claim, reported by Fox 13 News. One slider today.
src: Fox 13: New lie detector test finds deception through eye movement

firecam.condition: a fire, before anyone reports it
firecam.scenario: California: over 1,000 mountaintop cameras watch for smoke, with AI flagging new plumes to firefighters.
firecam.pos: get spotted before the first 911 call
firecam.says: 38 in 100 (636 of 1,668) were spotted before anyone called 911. The cameras caught 1,668 of Cal Fire’s 7,553 fires that year. Dust storms and clouds still fool them sometimes.
firecam.note: ALERTCalifornia and Cal Fire figures, reported by FireRescue1. One slider today.
src: FireRescue1: Over 1,000 AI cameras help spot California wildfires before the first 911 call

japaneew.test: Japan’s earthquake early warning, shaking forecast
japaneew.scenario: Japan: seconds after a quake starts, phones and TVs warn how strongly it will shake where you are.
japaneew.says: About 3 in 4 warnings predicted the shaking within one step of Japan’s intensity scale (72–82% in normal years). After the 2011 Tōhoku quake, a flood of aftershocks dropped it to 28%.
japaneew.note: Japan Meteorological Agency hit rates, 2007–2011, via Wikipedia. One slider today.

citrusdog.scenario: US orchards: dogs walk the rows sniffing for citrus greening, a bacterial disease that kills orange trees.
citrusdog.says: About 99 in 100, as early as two weeks after infection, when trees can look healthy for months or years. The rare false alarms were where a sick tree had once grown.
citrusdog.note: US Department of Agriculture research, reported by Modern Farmer (2020). One slider today.
src: Modern Farmer: Dogs could save the citrus industry from a devastating disease (2020)

winddog.condition: a bat downed by a turbine
winddog.scenario: California wind farms: researchers place bat and bird carcasses near turbines, then send searchers out the next day.
winddog.says: 96 in 100 (and 90% of small birds). Human searchers at a nearby wind farm found 6% of bats. The dogs suggest turbines affect bats far more than human surveys showed.
winddog.note: Smallwood et al., Journal of Wildlife Management (2020), reported by Smithsonian. One slider today.
src: Smithsonian: Dogs sniff out answers on bat and bird deaths near wind turbines

windhuman.test: Human searcher, finding bats at a wind farm
windhuman.condition: a bat downed by a turbine
windhuman.scenario: A trained person walks the ground under wind turbines looking for bats and birds placed there the day before.
windhuman.says: Just 6 in 100 bats (and 30% of small birds). A dog at the next wind farm found 96% of bats. Small, brown and lying in grass is hard for eyes, easy for noses.
windhuman.note: Smallwood et al., Journal of Wildlife Management (2020), reported by Smithsonian. One slider today.
src: Smithsonian: Dogs sniff out answers on bat and bird deaths near wind turbines

nbaref.scenario: Basketball: the NBA reviews every call and non-call in the last two minutes of close games and publishes the results.
nbaref.says: 86 in 100 in the first season of reports (1,864 plays, 135 games). The league’s boss said ‘roughly 90 percent’. Either way, about 1 in 7 is wrong when it matters most.
nbaref.note: Boston Globe analysis of the NBA’s Last Two Minute reports (2015); Adam Silver on ESPN. One slider today.
src: Boston Globe: In close games, how often do NBA referees get it right? (2015)
theScore: Silver says referees get roughly 90 percent of calls right

honey.scenario: 2022: EU anti-fraud investigators test 320 batches of honey imported into Europe for cheap added sugar syrups.
honey.says: Only 54 in 100. 46% were suspected of being bulked up with sugar syrup.
honey.note: European Anti-Fraud Office (OLAF) report 2023, operation ‘From the Hives’. One slider today.
src: OLAF report 2023: No money for fake honey
honey.label: Label check

oregano.scenario: UK, 2015: the consumer group Which? tests 78 jars and packets of dried oregano.
oregano.says: About 76 in 100. 19 of 78 contained other leaves, mostly olive and myrtle, making up 30–70% of the pack.
oregano.note: Which? survey reported by FoodNavigator (2015). One slider today.
src: FoodNavigator: Quarter of dried oregano contains other ingredients, Which? (2015)
oregano.label: Label check

laugh.test: Your ears, real laugh or fake?
laugh.condition: the right answer, real or fake
laugh.scenario: Listeners in 21 countries hear short clips of laughter, some genuine and some put on. Real or fake?
laugh.says: Between 56 and 69 in 100 depending on the country (Samoa lowest, Japan highest), from 884 listeners. Better than chance everywhere: a forced laugh is hard to hide.
laugh.note: Bryant et al., study across 21 societies (2018), reported by ScienceDaily. One slider today.
src: ScienceDaily: People across the world can tell real from fake laughter (2018)

turing.scenario: 2025 Turing test: you chat with two partners at once. One is a person; the other is GPT-4.5, told to play a persona. Which one is the bot?
turing.neg: pick the human as the bot
turing.says: Only 27 in 100: people picked GPT-4.5 as the human 73% of the time, more often than the actual human. Meta’s LLaMa fooled them 56% of the time.
turing.note: UC San Diego study (2025): 284 participants, 1,023 games, reported by Live Science. One slider today.
src: Live Science: GPT-4.5 is the first AI model to pass an authentic Turing test, scientists say (2025)

violin.test: Top soloist, Stradivarius or new violin?
violin.condition: the right answer, old or new
violin.scenario: A blind test: ten world-class violin soloists play old Italian violins, Stradivaris included, alongside new ones, then guess which is which.
violin.says: About 45 in 100 (31 right, 33 wrong, 5 unsure). No better than chance, from people who play for a living.
violin.note: Fritz et al., PNAS (2014), reported by The Strad. One slider today.
src: The Strad: Blind-tested soloists unable to tell Stradivarius violins from modern instruments

fakenews.test: Your gut, spotting a fake headline
fakenews.scenario: Late 2016: a survey shows US adults some of the most-shared fake news headlines of the election. Those who remember seeing one: did they think it was accurate?
fakenews.says: Only about 25 in 100: fake headlines fooled people about 75% of the time. Familiarity feels a lot like truth.
fakenews.note: Ipsos survey of 3,015 US adults for BuzzFeed News (2016), via Media Matters. One slider today.
src: Media Matters: BuzzFeed, most Americans who see fake news believe it (2016)

abs.condition: a wrong ball or strike call
abs.scenario: Major League Baseball, 2026: players can challenge the umpire’s ball-or-strike call, and an automated tracking system (ABS) decides on the spot.
abs.says: 54 in 100 (5,686 of 10,557). Catchers did best at 59%, batters 49%, pitchers 40%. So umpires were wrong about half the time a player felt sure.
abs.note: MLB’s first ABS challenge season, reported by TSN. One slider today.
src: TSN: Robot umpires flip 54% of challenged calls in ABS debut season (2026)

mlbreplay.scenario: Major League Baseball, 2022: a manager challenges a call on the field (safe or out, fair or foul) and video replay decides.
mlbreplay.says: Almost exactly a coin toss: 633 of 1,261 (50.2%). Managers have staff watching replays before they challenge, and still miss half.
mlbreplay.note: MLB figures for the 2022 season, reported by NBC Sports. One slider today.
src: NBC Sports: Half of MLB video review challenges led to overturned calls (2022)

rekognition.scenario: 2018: a civil liberties group runs photos of every member of the US Congress through Amazon’s face-recognition tool against 25,000 arrest photos.
rekognition.says: About 95 in 100: it falsely matched 28 members (out of 535) with arrest photos, and members of colour were wrongly matched disproportionately.
rekognition.note: ACLU test of Amazon Rekognition at default settings (2018). One slider today.
src: ACLU: Amazon facial surveillance technology falsely identifies 28 members of Congress with mugshots (2018)

astrology.test: Astrologer, matching a birth chart to its owner
astrology.scenario: A double-blind test: astrologers get a person’s birth chart plus three personality profiles, one of them the real person’s. Pick the match.
astrology.says: About 33 in 100, exactly what you’d get by guessing from three. The astrologers had predicted at least 50%.
astrology.note: Shawn Carlson’s test, published in Nature (1985), described by The Skeptic. One slider today.
src: The Skeptic: From the archives, a sceptical look at astrology

nhloffside.test: Ice hockey coach’s challenge for offside
nhloffside.condition: a goal that should be disallowed
nhloffside.scenario: NHL: a goal is scored, and the other coach challenges, saying an attacker crossed the blue line too early.
nhloffside.says: 86 in 100 (108 of 126) in 2023–24. Goalie-interference challenges worked 54% of the time and stoppage challenges 27%. Offside is easy to see on a freeze-frame.
nhloffside.note: Scouting the Refs, NHL coach’s challenge tracker, 2023–24 regular season. One slider today.
src: Scouting the Refs: Coach’s challenges for 2023–24 regular season

koaladrone.scenario: Queensland: a drone with a thermal camera flies over bushland and AI picks out koala-shaped warm spots in the trees.
koaladrone.says: About 86 in 100, against about 70 for an expert spotter on the ground. Koalas are grey, still and high up, but they are warm.
koaladrone.note: Queensland University of Technology team, reported by Mongabay (2019). One slider today.
src: Mongabay: AI and drone-based imagery improve survey power for cryptic animals (2019)

koalaspotter.scenario: An experienced koala spotter walks through bushland, scanning the treetops for koalas.
koalaspotter.says: About 70 in 100, according to the drone researchers. Their heat-seeking drone with AI found about 86.
koalaspotter.note: Queensland University of Technology team, reported by Mongabay (2019). One slider today.
src: Mongabay: AI and drone-based imagery improve survey power for cryptic animals (2019)

poems.test: Your gut, AI poem or real poet?
poems.condition: the right answer, AI or human
poems.scenario: Readers see poems by Shakespeare, Chaucer, Whitman, Dickinson, Plath and others, mixed with AI imitations in their style.
poems.says: About 46 in 100, slightly worse than guessing, from 1,634 readers. They even preferred the AI verse.
poems.note: Porter and Machery (2024), reported by Smithsonian. One slider today.
src: Smithsonian: ChatGPT or Shakespeare? Readers couldn’t tell the difference (2024)

aidet14.test: AI-text detectors (14 tools), on raw ChatGPT
aidet14.scenario: Researchers test 14 AI-text detectors, Turnitin and GPTZero included, on human writing and on untouched ChatGPT text.
aidet14.says: They caught about 74 in 100 untouched ChatGPT texts and correctly cleared 96 in 100 human ones. Decent on clean text. Now see what a few edits do.
aidet14.note: Weber-Wulff et al. (2023), reported by MIT Technology Review before peer review.
src: MIT Technology Review: AI-text detection tools are really easy to fool (2023)

aidetedit.test: AI-text detectors, on lightly edited ChatGPT
aidetedit.scenario: Same 14 detectors, but this time the ChatGPT text has been tweaked slightly by a human.
aidetedit.says: A few tweaks and detection fell to 42 in 100, while still clearing 96 in 100 human texts. A thesaurus beats most detectors.
aidetedit.note: Weber-Wulff et al. (2023), reported by MIT Technology Review before peer review.
src: MIT Technology Review: AI-text detection tools are really easy to fool (2023)

floodpeak.scenario: A river is rising after heavy rain. Australia’s Bureau of Meteorology forecasts how high it will peak, typically aiming to be within 30 cm.
floodpeak.says: 73 in 100 met the target in 2025–26, and 65% gave the warning time promised. Rivers are harder to call than tomorrow’s top temperature.
floodpeak.note: Bureau of Meteorology performance figures, 2025–26. One slider today.
floodpeak.label: Forecast

windfc.scenario: Australia’s Bureau of Meteorology forecasts tomorrow’s wind speed at hundreds of places. Counts as right if within 5 knots (about 10 km/h).
windfc.says: About 91 in 100 nationally, up from about 83 in 2015. Coastal spots are harder: 86.7%.
windfc.note: Bureau of Meteorology performance figures, 2025–26. One slider today.
windfc.label: Forecast

mintemp.scenario: Australia’s Bureau of Meteorology forecasts the overnight minimum at about 500 places. Counts as right if within 2°C.
mintemp.says: About 83 in 100, versus 91 for the daytime maximum. Overnight lows are trickier than daytime highs.
mintemp.note: Bureau of Meteorology performance figures, 2025–26. One slider today.
mintemp.label: Forecast

drs.scenario: Test cricket: a player is sure the umpire got it wrong and asks for the Decision Review System: replays, ball-tracking and edge detection.
drs.says: Only about 26 in 100, across 2,100+ Test reviews to 2017. Batters did better (34%) than bowling sides (about 20%). Umpires are better than players think.
drs.note: ESPNcricinfo analysis of Test reviews, November 2009 to March 2017. One slider today.
src: ESPNcricinfo: The art of the review (2017)

tortoise.scenario: Mojave Desert, US: dog teams and human teams search the same ground for threatened desert tortoises.
tortoise.says: About 70 in 100, and no better than the human teams. Dogs were 2.5 hours a day faster and better at finding tortoises in bushes; humans were about $3,000 cheaper per square kilometre.
tortoise.note: Nussear et al. (2008), US Geological Survey. One slider today.
src: USGS: Are wildlife detector dogs or people better at finding desert tortoises?

birdnet.test: BirdNET, listening to a city recorder
birdnet.condition: a bird species that’s really calling
birdnet.scenario: Munich: sound recorders run at a city site and the free BirdNET AI lists every species it hears. Experts check the recordings.
birdnet.says: About 79 in 100 species picked up, and 95% of what it reported was right. The researchers said it can be as good as experts.
birdnet.note: Munich study (bioRxiv preprint, 2024), best settings, whole-dataset level. One slider today.
src: bioRxiv: BirdNET can be as good as experts for acoustic bird monitoring in a European city (2024)

sheep.scenario: Cambridge, 2017: sheep learn photos of celebrities’ faces, then have to pick a familiar face from a pair.
sheep.says: About 8 times in 10, against 50% for guessing. Eight Welsh Mountain sheep, and their accuracy fell with tilted photos, much as ours does.
sheep.note: University of Cambridge study (2017), reported by PBS NOVA. One slider today.
src: PBS NOVA: These sheep learned to recognise pictures of Obama and other celebrities (2017)
sheep.label: Animal

archerfish.scenario: Archerfish, which knock insects down with a jet of water, learn one human face, then must aim at it when it’s shown among new faces.
archerfish.says: 81 to 86 in 100 across two experiments, picking it out from up to 44 new faces, even with head shape and colour standardised. Even fish can do faces.
archerfish.note: University of Queensland and Oxford study (2016). One slider today.
src: UQ News: You fish can recognise human faces (2016)
archerfish.label: Animal

beefaces.scenario: 2005: honeybees are rewarded with sugar water for visiting one particular photo of a human face, then tested with others.
beefaces.says: Better than 80 in 100 (one bee hit 94%). Two days later, two bees still scored 79% and 76%. Not bad for an insect.
beefaces.note: Dyer et al., Journal of Experimental Biology (2005), reported by phys.org. One slider today.
src: phys.org: Bees can recognise human faces, study finds (2005)
beefaces.label: Animal

dogvoice.test: Dog, finding its owner by voice
dogvoice.scenario: 2022: dogs hear recordings of their owner’s voice and strangers’ voices. Can they find the owner by voice alone?
dogvoice.says: 82 in 100. Dogs found their owner by voice alone in 82% of trials. Worth a treat.
dogvoice.note: Study reported by Fox 9 (2022). One slider today.
src: Fox 9: Dogs can recognise their owners just by their voice, study finds (2022)
dogvoice.label: Animal

googleassistant.scenario: 2019: 800 everyday questions are asked out loud to Google Assistant on a phone.
googleassistant.says: 93 in 100, and it understood all 800. Siri managed 83% and Alexa 80%.
googleassistant.note: Loup Ventures digital assistant test (2019), reported by CNBC. One slider today.
src: CNBC: Google Assistant beats Siri and Alexa in IQ test as all three improve (2019)

alexa.scenario: 2019: the same 800 everyday questions are asked out loud to Amazon’s Alexa.
alexa.says: 80 in 100, behind Siri (83%) and Google Assistant (93%). It misunderstood only one question; it just didn’t always know the answer.
alexa.note: Loup Ventures digital assistant test (2019), reported by CNBC. One slider today.
src: CNBC: Google Assistant beats Siri and Alexa in IQ test as all three improve (2019)

knapweed.scenario: US: dogs are trained to sniff out spotted knapweed, an invasive weed, so it can be pulled before it spreads.
knapweed.says: About 93 in 100 overall, and 98% in the final open-field trials.
knapweed.note: Studies of knapweed detection dogs, cited in Wikipedia’s detection dog article. One slider today.
